body.heading: Letters that keep quiet
paragraphs: Most letters do their job out loud. But some letters stand in a word and say nothing at all. The k in knight does not make a sound. Neither does the b in thumb or the w in write.
Hundreds of years ago, people DID pronounce those letters — a knight was a 'kuh-nicht'! The spelling stayed, the sound left, and now we just have to learn the quiet ones by sight.

body.heading: Silent k and g: knight's family
paragraphs: knight, knife, knee, knock, know — the k is silent; say only the n.
gnome, gnat, gnaw — the g is silent; say only the n.

body.heading: Silent b and w
paragraphs: thumb, lamb, climb, comb — the b is silent at the end.
write, wrong, wrist, wrap — the w is silent at the start.
answer, sword — here the w hides in the middle!

body.heading: Silent h and t
paragraphs: hour, honest, heir — the h is silent; say 'our', 'onest', 'air'.
listen, often (for many speakers), castle, whistle — the t keeps quiet too.

body.heading: Think and talk
paragraphs: 1. Why do you think English kept the silent letters instead of fixing the spelling? (Hint: books were printed with the old spellings, and printing froze them in place.)
2. Invent a sentence using three silent-letter words — then read it to someone and see if they can spell the tricky words.

takeaway: Silent letters — the k in knight, b in thumb, w in write, h in hour — are leftovers from old pronunciations; learn them by eye and they lose their power to trip you.
materials: Just you and this page — no materials needed
